content: 1. As multiple vaccine products become available, it is essential to identify those vaccines that have a more significant impact on controlling severe and serious diseases. This requires monitoring long-term epidemiological trends, particularly the co-circulation of similar viruses and pathogens. 2. Surveillance systems for respiratory viruses with epidemic and pandemic potential, such as influenza, should be implemented as coordinated and collaborative systems. These systems must align with specific priority objectives and include associated investigations and studies. 3. For further guidance on developing pandemic disease surveillance programs, refer to the WHO’s 2023 framework titled “Crafting the Mosaic: A Framework for Resilient Surveillance for Respiratory Viruses of Epidemic and Pandemic Potential.” 4. Pandemic preparedness plans should include an extended section on pandemic surveillance approaches, as recommended by the WHO. 5. Countries should establish surveillance systems using standardized case definitions and investigation protocols to collect essential information from suspected cases. This data enables evidence-based public health actions, such as tracking the time from symptom onset to peak and outcomes like death, discharge, or referral. 6. Surveillance systems should also collect data on potential viral, bacterial, and fungal co-infections, including whether testing for co-infections was conducted and under what conditions. 7. Countries must ensure the collection of relevant clinical specimens in accordance with global and national surveillance guidelines for recommended laboratory testing. 8. Surveillance data requirements may evolve as the pandemic progresses. These requirements should be guided by vaccination program needs and the necessity to monitor the pandemic disease. 9. Countries are requested to share collected pandemic disease surveillance data with the WHO regularly. This facilitates a global understanding of vaccine effectiveness and its impact on the pandemic. 10. Evaluating vaccine effectiveness contributes to the evidence base for developing vaccination policies and strategies for a sustained pandemic response. This is particularly important in the context of potential vaccine escape or waning immunity. 11. Various study designs can be employed to evaluate vaccine effectiveness in real-world settings. Existing sentinel surveillance systems for severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) or influenza-like illness (ILI) may be leveraged for this purpose, provided there is adequate vaccine uptake in the population. 12. Networks of countries may need to pool data to achieve robust sample sizes for vaccine effectiveness evaluations. 13. Impact evaluations aim to estimate the number of events averted by vaccination, such as reductions in incidence, hospitalizations, and deaths. Cost estimations can also assess the cost-effectiveness of vaccination programs. 14. Surveillance data for pandemic diseases enables public health authorities to adjust and guide vaccination activities. This includes defining priority populations, determining vaccine doses required, optimizing intervals between doses, and assessing the need for booster doses, hospital beds, and curative services. 15. Countries should develop disease pandemic surveillance systems or utilize existing influenza surveillance mechanisms to collect key epidemiological, virological, clinical, and immunization data for evidence-based decision-making. 16. Surveillance teams should work closely with immunization teams to ensure the effective use of surveillance data in shaping vaccination activities. 17. Termination of pandemic vaccination operations is an official part of deployment activities and must be planned with necessary steps and stakeholder involvement. This includes releasing surge staff, returning unused resources, and documenting lessons learned. 18. Following the official announcement of the end of a pandemic by the WHO, national public health authorities should issue a statement confirming their intention to conclude response operations. Resources used, best practices observed, and challenges faced should be documented to improve future pandemic responses. 19. Managers responsible for vaccine stock tracking should complete their tasks promptly. Reports should include the number of unused vaccine doses and quantities of ancillary supplies at each distribution point. 20. Data on vaccination sites, vaccine doses received and administered, human resources deployed, communication activities, and logistics should be collated from micro-plans and local management systems. 21. Termination reports should document the technical, logistical, and financial aspects of vaccine deployment and vaccination activities, including coverage for key groups. The report should also describe how vaccines were approved, procured, and deployed, as well as plans for healthcare waste management. 22. Evaluating the impact of introducing a new vaccine during and after a pandemic is critical for achieving programmatic goals and improving future pandemic preparedness and response. 23. WHO recommends two types of post-introduction evaluations (PIE) for pandemic vaccination programs: a mini-PIE and a full PIE. These evaluations aim to identify lessons learned and actionable results to improve vaccine roll-out. 24. Simulation exercises during inter-pandemic periods can enhance coordination among stakeholders and identify areas of pandemic vaccine deployment plans that require revision. 25. WHO organizes regional workshops to exchange best practices and lessons learned between countries, including simulation exercises. Countries should assess whether similar practices can be introduced in their settings.
